sec.title: Background and Objectives:
sec.p: Cognitive impairments in the executive and visuospatial domains are common after ischemic stroke and significantly affect a patient’s independence. These impairments can affect problem-solving abilities, planning, decision-making, and spatial awareness, which are critical for functional recovery. Understanding the trajectory of recovery and its association with functional outcomes is essential for improving the quality of life of stroke survivors. The Objectives of the study are to evaluate the recovery patterns of executive and visuospatial functions 90 days after ischemic stroke and to examine their relationship with functional outcomes.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: In this longitudinal study, 401 patients with neuroimaging-confirmed ischemic stroke were assessed at admission and on Days 7, 30, and 90 post-stroke. Executive function was measured using the alternate Trail Making Test, and visuospatial function was assessed using the cube-copying and clock-drawing tests. Functional outcomes were evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Barthel Index. Repeated measures ANOVA (analysis of variance) was employed to assess cognitive recovery over time, and Spearman’s correlation was used to examine the relationship between cognitive and functional outcomes.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Significant improvements in executive and visuospatial functions were observed over the 90-day period, with the greatest gains noted within the first 30 days. A moderate-to-strong negative correlation between mRS and cognitive function was identified at all time points, peaking on Day 7.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Executive and visuospatial functions show dynamic recovery in the first 90 days post-stroke, particularly during the acute and subacute phases. Functional disability is closely associated with cognitive performance, underscoring the importance of early cognitive assessment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Ischemic stroke is one of the leading causes of long-term disability, significantly affecting the quality of life of survivors and placing considerable demands on caregivers and healthcare systems. Cognitive impairments, particularly in executive and visuospatial functions, represent some of the most challenging outcomes, as these areas are essential for performing daily activities and preserving independence.[12] These impairments result from localized cortical and subcortical brain lesions that disrupt neuronal networks essential for higher-order cognitive processes.[34]

Visuospatial functions encompass the skills necessary for spatial awareness and the ability to pursue, integrate, and interpret visual information to guide actions, whereas executive functions involve processes such as problem-solving, goal-oriented behavior, decision-making, and adaptation to dynamic environments.[5] Stroke-related disruption of these intricate networks leads to significant cognitive and functional impairments, particularly when lesions involve the frontal lobe, parietal lobe, and subcortical structures.[6]

The trajectory of executive and visuospatial function recovery following ischemic stroke is highly dynamic and influenced by several intrinsic and extrinsic factors, including stroke severity, lesion location, patient age, education level, comorbidities, and the quality and intensity of rehabilitation interventions.[789] Despite substantial advancements in understanding language and motor recovery, nuanced changes in executive and visuospatial recovery remain understudied.[10] Understanding these changes is critical, as executive and visuospatial functions influence problem-solving, planning, and navigation, which are key aspects of reintegration into personal, social, and professional life.

This study aimed to address this gap by evaluating the recovery trajectories of executive and visuospatial functions in patients with ischemic stroke. It also aimed to provide information about cognitive recovery and its correlation with functional recovery over time by analyzing the recovery trajectory through longitudinal assessment.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This prospective longitudinal study was conducted at a tertiary care center in South India between February 2020 and November 2022. Adults aged ≥18 years with a confirmed diagnosis of ischemic stroke on neuroimaging were recruited following informed consent. Patients with significant pre-existing visual impairments unrelated to stroke were excluded to ensure a valid visuospatial assessment. This study was registered with the Clinical Trials Registry- India (CTRI) (CTRI/2020/01/022783). Ethical approval was obtained from the Kasturba Medical College and Kasturba Hospital Institutional Ethics Committee (approval number: 246/2019) to conduct the study.

sec.title: Cognitive and functional assessments
sec.p: Cognitive function was evaluated using standardized clinical tools. Executive functioning was assessed using the Alternate Trail Making Test, which required participants to alternate between numeric and alphabetic sequences. Visuospatial function was measured using the cube copying and clock drawing tests, with a composite score derived from performance across all tests. Each cognitive task was scored as binary (0 = incorrect, 1 = correct), with a cumulative score range of 0–5.[111]

Functional outcomes were assessed using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) and Barthel Index, both of which are validated tools for evaluating disability and independence in activities of daily living. Demographic, clinical, and radiological data were collected at baseline.

sec.title: Data collection and follow-up
sec.p: Participants were evaluated at four time points: admission (baseline), Day 7, Day 30, and Day 90 post-stroke. All assessments were conducted by trained personnel following a standardized protocol. Medical management and physiotherapy were provided according to institutional guidelines; however, the rehabilitation intensity was not quantitatively assessed.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the baseline characteristics. Changes in cognitive function over time were analyzed using repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA), with post-hoc Tukey’s tests identifying significant pairwise differences. Spearman’s rank correlation assessed the relationship between cognitive scores and mRS at each follow-up point. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05. Analyses were performed using EZR (Easy R statistical software version 1.61).

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The study included 401 eligible patients with ischemic stroke who were admitted to the neurology ward between February 2020 and November 2022. The average age of the cohort was 62.3±12.45 (Mean ± standard deviation) years, with a male predominance of 277 patients (69.1%). Unemployment was present in 177 (43.9%) patients, and the median Kuppuswamy socioeconomic scale score was 13.00 (Interquartile Range [IQR]: 3.00–27.00) [Table 1]. The most prevalent comorbidities were hypertension and diabetes mellitus, affecting 65.6% and 41.6% of the patients, respectively [Table 2].

sec.p: Infarctions were more common in the left cerebral hemisphere, affecting 172 (42.9%) of the patients. The left middle cerebral artery (MCA) was involved in 111 patients (27.8%) and the right MCA in 84 patients (20.9%). The basal ganglia (47.1%) and frontal lobe (46.1%) were the most frequently affected brain regions [Table 2]. The median visuospatial and executive function scores were zero at admission but improved to 2 (IQR: 0–5) by Days 30 and 90 post-stroke [Table 3].

sec.title: Recovery trajectory of executive and visuospatial functions
sec.p: The recovery trajectory of executive and visuospatial functions was assessed at four key time points: admission (Level 1), Day 7 (Level 2), Day 30 (Level 3), and Day 90 (Level 4) post-stroke. Repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of time on recovery outcomes (F [3,771] = 101, P < 0.001), indicating progressive improvement over time. The estimated marginal means demonstrated a steady increase, with values of 0.922 ± 0.0824 at admission, 1.512 ± 0.0945 on Day 7, 1.829 ± 0.0934 on Day 30, and 2.298 ± 0.0894 on Day 90. Post-hoc Tukey’s test revealed significant differences between all time points. Early improvement was most pronounced, as evidenced by the significant mean difference between Levels 1 and 2 (−0.589, P < 0.001). Continued recovery was observed between Levels 2 and 3 (−0.318, P < 0.001) and between Levels 3 and 4 (−0.469, P < 0.001), although the rate of improvement slowed over time [Table 4].

sec.title: Relationships between executive and visuospatial function and functional outcomes in ischemic stroke patients
sec.p: This study explored the relationship between functional outcomes, measured using the mRS, and executive and visuospatial function at admission and during follow-ups on Days 7, 30, and 90 post-stroke. A significant negative correlation was observed at all time points, indicating that greater functional disability was associated with poorer executive and visuospatial functions. At admission, a moderate negative correlation (ρ = −0.34, P = 3.15 × 10−12) indicated that patients with more severe disability exhibited lower cognitive performance. By Day 7, the correlation strengthened (ρ = −0.434, P < 0.001), suggesting that functional impairments during the acute phase had a pronounced effect on cognitive domains. This strong association persisted on Day 30 (ρ = −0.423, P = 1.58 × 10 − 15), emphasizing the continued interplay between physical disability and cognitive recovery in the subacute phase. By Day 90, the correlation weakened slightly but remained significant (ρ = −0.241, P = 0.0000381), demonstrating that functional impairments continued to influence cognitive outcomes in the 90-day post-stroke phase, although to a lesser degree [Table 5 and Figure 1a-d].

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study evaluated the recovery trajectories of executive and visuospatial functions in patients with ischemic stroke over 90 days and explored their association with functional outcomes. The results highlighted a dynamic, time-dependent recovery pattern, with significant gains observed mainly in the early post-stroke period.

Our findings corroborate previous evidence that executive and visuospatial impairments are prevalent immediately after a stroke and tend to improve with time. The most substantial improvement occurred between admission and Day 30, aligning with the neuroplasticity window often observed during early stroke recovery.[12] Evidence suggests that the recovery trajectory is often nonlinear, with rapid improvements occurring during the acute and subacute phases, followed by a plateau in the chronic phase. Furthermore, another study suggested that the early recovery of visuospatial functions is often less pronounced than that of executive functions because of the complexity of the neural networks involved.[13]

The moderate-to-strong negative correlation between the mRS and cognitive scores at all time points reinforces the interconnectedness of physical and cognitive recovery. Notably, the strongest correlation on Day 7 suggests that functional disability during the acute phase may significantly impact early cognitive performance. Although the correlation was attenuated by Day 90, it remained statistically significant, indicating a persistent relationship. The slightly weaker correlation at Day 90 in our study aligns with existing research, which concluded that physical recovery may outpace cognitive recovery in some patients with ischemic stroke. The study reported that while physical disability often shows marked improvement by 3 months post-stroke, cognitive deficits, particularly in higher-order functions, may persist.[14]

The demographic characteristics of the cohort provided valuable insights into the socioeconomic and educational factors influencing patients with ischemic stroke. The age of the participants was consistent with that reported in previous studies, which observed a similar age range among ischemic stroke populations worldwide.[1415] The male predominance in this cohort aligns with findings from large-scale epidemiological studies, including the Global Burden of Stroke 2016 report, which noted a higher stroke incidence among men than among women.[15]

Hypertension and diabetes mellitus were identified as significant risk factors in the present study. This finding aligns with the observations of Lavy et al.,[16] who reported a high prevalence of these conditions among patients with stroke. Additionally, the present study revealed a higher incidence of infarctions in the left cerebral hemisphere. Previous studies have similarly demonstrated that left hemisphere infarctions are more frequent than right hemisphere infarctions, particularly among young adults, potentially due to the higher prevalence of atherosclerosis in the left carotid artery.[17] Another study reported a higher percentage of left hemisphere involvement in cerebral infections.[18] Our study found that the MCA was the most commonly affected vascular territory, consistent with existing literature identifying the MCA as the most frequently involved vessel in ischemic stroke.[19]

sec.title: Strengths and limitations
sec.p: The strengths of this study include its large sample size, longitudinal design, and use of validated assessment tools. However, the limitations of this study must be acknowledged. The single-center setting may limit the generalizability of our findings. Rehabilitation intensity was not quantified, and a more granular assessment of lesion characteristics and neural imaging markers could further elucidate the mechanisms underlying recovery.

sec.title: Future recommendations
sec.p: Future research should consider multicenter designs, incorporate neuroimaging correlates, and explore personalized rehabilitation strategies based on lesion profiles and baseline cognitive status.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The present study underscores the need for early identification and targeted rehabilitation of executive and visuospatial deficits in stroke survivors. Integrating cognitive evaluation into routine stroke care may enhance cognitive and functional recovery, ultimately improving patients’ long-term outcomes and quality of life.
